title: The N+1 problem
summary: One query for the list, one more for every item: spot it in the logged SQL and fix it with Include or a projection.

steps.title: One plus N
body: The most common EF Core performance bug looks innocent:
var count = db.Books.Count(b => b.AuthorId == author.Id);        // 1 query per author

One query fetches N authors, then the loop runs N more: **N+1 queries**. With 3 authors you will never notice. With 2,000 authors behind a web page, each round trip costing a millisecond or more, the page takes seconds, and the database is busy answering the same small question over and over.

It hides in many shapes: a query inside a loop, explicit `Load()` per item, lazy loading (each first touch of `author.Books` is a query), or a helper method called per row that "just" looks something up.
**Always look at the SQL a page runs.** If the number of commands grows with the number of rows, you have N+1.

answer: SQL> SELECT "a"."Id", "a"."Name" FROM "Authors" AS "a" ORDER BY "a"."Id"
SQL> SELECT COUNT(*) FROM "Books" AS "b" WHERE "b"."AuthorId" = @a_Id
SQL> SELECT COUNT(*) FROM "Books" AS "b" WHERE "b"."AuthorId" = @a_Id
SQL> SELECT COUNT(*) FROM "Books" AS "b" WHERE "b"."AuthorId" = @a_Id
steps.explain: One `SELECT` for the authors, then one `COUNT(*)` per author: 1 + 3 commands. Notice the parameter `@a_Id`: the same SQL runs again and again with a different value. That repetition is the signature of N+1.

steps.title: Two fixes
body: **Fix 1: load the related data with the list** (`Include`). One query with a join:
**Fix 2: project exactly what the page needs.** One query, and only the numbers cross the wire, not every book:
SELECT "a"."Name", (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM "Books" AS "b" WHERE "a"."Id" = "b"."AuthorId") AS "Books"

For read-only screens the projection is usually best: one round trip, small rows, no tracking. Use `Include` when you need the entities themselves (to change them, or because the page really shows all their data).

steps.explain: Anything that queries per item is N+1. Loading everything in one query, or fetching all the needed keys in one `IN (...)` query before the loop, is not.

steps.prompt: A page shows 50 orders and, for each, the customer's name. Which is the best fix for an N+1 that loads each customer separately?
options: Cache every customer in a static dictionary forever
Run the 50 customer queries in parallel
steps.explain: A projection gets everything in one query with a join, and only the columns the page shows. Caching and parallel queries treat the symptom, and lazy loading is the cause in disguise.

steps.prompt: How would you notice an N+1 in a running production app?
options: Count database commands per request in your logs or tracing; a count that grows with the data is the sign
It throws an exception once there are too many queries
EF Core refuses to run more than 100 queries per context
The C# compiler warns about queries in loops
steps.explain: Nothing fails: the page just gets slower as data grows. Logging `CommandExecuted` events, or OpenTelemetry tracing, makes the repeated identical statements visible.

steps.title: Fix the N+1
prompt: This report works, but runs one query per author **and** one per book. Rewrite it to run **exactly one** command, returning the same lines (authors by name; books by title; average stars to one decimal, or `-` with no reviews).
class Author { int Id; string Name; List<Book> Books; }
class Book   { int Id; string Title; int Year; int AuthorId; Author Author; List<Review> Reviews; List<Tag> Tags; }
class Review { int Id; int Stars; int BookId; }
class Tag    { int Id; string Name; List<Book> Books; }
Four books: Earthsea (Le Guin, 1968, 2 reviews), The Dispossessed (Le Guin, 1974, 1 review), Dune (Herbert, 1965, 3 reviews), Emma (Austen, 1815, no reviews).
starter: var books = db.Books.Where(b => b.AuthorId == author.Id).OrderBy(b => b.Title).ToList();
var stars = db.Books.Where(b => b.Id == book.Id).SelectMany(b => b.Reviews).Select(r => r.Stars).ToList();
